scope: Short, curated research summaries. Not a medical protocol library or systematic review.

chunks.title: Spaceflight-induced bone changes
chunks.text: Reduced skeletal loading in microgravity is associated with changes in weight-bearing bones. NASA identifies bone changes as an exploration health concern and notes remaining questions about longer missions and recovery.

chunks.title: Bone monitoring and countermeasures
chunks.section: What can be done about it?
chunks.text: NASA describes preflight and postflight bone scans and research on resistive exercise as part of understanding and limiting bone changes. These observations concern bone measurements, not a camera-derived diagnosis.

chunks.title: Gravity transitions and functional performance
chunks.text: Changing gravity environments can affect orientation, coordination, balance, and locomotion. NASA uses functional task testing to study performance after landing on a gravitational surface.

chunks.title: Muscle and bone assessment
chunks.text: NASA describes muscle mass changes in microgravity and uses imaging and fitness evaluations to investigate physical changes. A joint-motion observation alone does not identify the cause of an individual's change.

chunks.title: Distance from Earth and onboard capability
chunks.text: Mars exploration introduces communication delays and limits resupply. NASA studies medical data architectures, decision support, crew training, and onboard resources to support more independent operations.

chunks.title: Human performance and countermeasure design
chunks.text: NASA human-performance requirements address physical capability and exercise countermeasures in mission design. Equipment, individual condition, and operational context matter. This source is not an individualized exercise prescription.

chunks.title: Individual space-radiation monitoring
chunks.text: NASA calls for individual monitoring of crew radiation exposure because absorbed dose varies with crew activity. Mission duration or location alone is not a personal dose measurement, and a dosimeter reading does not establish bone-specific dose or explain a movement change.
